canonical_statement: Recurrent ischemic events were prospectively counted from 24 hours after thrombolytic administration until death, coronary revascularization, or 24 hours after heparin discontinuation.
Creatine kinase and CK isoenzymes were measured on admission, every 4 hours for 24 hours, then daily for 2 days.
Continuous variables were compared with a 2-sample t test, categorical variables with chi-square testing, and group means were reported as mean plus or minus the standard error of the mean.

The association between PTT level and recurrent ischemia was analyzed with the Mann-Whitney test after PTT values were assigned to 4 arbitrarily determined ranges without knowledge of the distribution of ischemic events; p<0.05 was considered significant.

Three of the 75 thrombolysis-treated patients were excluded from analysis, leaving 72 patients: one lacked confirmatory AMI evidence, one underwent CABG within 24 hours, and one did not receive post-thrombolysis heparin after intervening cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
The analyzed cohort had a mean age of 57.5 ± 1.2 years (SEM).

canonical_statement: The authors attributed the absence of new late bleeding complications to the possibility that the observed early hemorrhagic events were related more to thrombolytic-associated hemostatic abnormalities than to heparin itself.

Because 8 recurrent ischemic events occurred within 24 hours after cessation of heparin, the authors concluded that the indication for and timing of heparin discontinuation after thrombolytic therapy should be carefully assessed.

The authors interpreted the earlier thrombolytic treatment and earlier CK peak among patients with recurrent ischemia as supportive of recurrent ischemia being a marker of reperfusion and myocardial salvage.

Although PTT values >100 seconds were associated with the fewest recurrent ischemic episodes, therapeutic anticoagulation did not prevent all ischemia; the authors concluded that anticoagulation intensity is only one determinant of recurrent ischemic risk.
The authors reported no difference in the percentage of residual coronary stenosis between patients with and without recurrent ischemia.

The authors speculated that antiplatelet therapy combined with heparin or reduction of residual stenosis by angioplasty might be more effective for preventing recurrent ischemia than heparin anticoagulation alone.

The paper concluded that lower heparin anticoagulation levels were associated with more recurrent ischemic events, that heparin discontinuation was frequently followed by ischemia, and that heparin administration was associated with a low observed incidence of hemorrhagic complications.
